headline: A Squid Bait, Fifteen Hundred Feet Down, and a Broadbill Off Oceanographer
subhead: The swordfish bite we flagged last week held up, the bluefin still won't cooperate, and the run math out east hasn't gotten any shorter.
body_markdown:
The radio chatter out of the canyon fleet this week has had one word in it more than any other: broadbill. A boat running out of Montauk called in Tuesday afternoon with a daytime drop connection somewhere out past the edge, live squid bait down deep, and a swordfish on the deck before lunch. That's not a fluke story anymore — it's the third week running we've heard variations of it, and it lines up with what we said here last week: watch the swordfish activity out this way, because it's been a standout and worth tracking hard. Here it is, still going.

The pattern is simple enough to explain even if it isn't simple to execute. Daytime swordfishing means dropping a rig — squid, glow gear, weight enough to get down fast — through the water column until you find the thermocline the fish are stacked under, often thirteen, fourteen, fifteen hundred feet depending on the day and the structure. Oceanographer has been the address this week. Whether that holds at Hydrographer or slides toward Veatch as the week goes is the open question, and it's the kind of thing you don't know until a boat's actually out there with a rig in the water. If you're rigging for it, bring patience and bring fuel — this isn't a drive-by.

Which gets to the part of this job nobody glamorizes: the run. Out of Montauk, Block, or the Rhode Island ports, you're not popping over to these canyons on a whim. Atlantis is the closest of the bunch and it still eats the better part of a tank getting there and back before you've wet a line. Push out to Veatch, Hydrographer, or Oceanographer and you're committing the boat and the day to it — fuel burn on the way out, fuel burn on the standby drift, fuel burn getting home in whatever sea builds through the afternoon. Nobody complains about it because complaining doesn't shorten the ride. You just do the math before you leave the dock, and this week the math has favored the boats willing to make the full run rather than split the difference somewhere shy of the edge.

Bluefin, meanwhile, remain the disappointment of the season so far — not a surprise, just the honest read. This is the part of the fall calendar where bluefin activity typically softens up before the November run gets going again, and that's exactly what's happening. Trollers working spreads of green machines and cedar plugs around the canyon edges have picked at fish here and there, but nothing that resembles a pattern worth chasing hard. If bluefin are your target this week, temper the expectations and treat any fish as a bonus rather than the plan.

On the yellowfin, white marlin, mahi, and wahoo front — the usual fall cast of characters out here — there's no strong signal to report yet this week specifically for this stretch of canyons. That doesn't mean they're not around; it means nobody's called in a pattern solid enough to put in print. Worth keeping gear rigged for a mahi under any floating debris you cross on the way out, and a naked ballyhoo or two in the spread never hurts on the troll, but the story this week isn't tuna or billfish. It's broadbill.

For tactics on the swordfish drop, the boats having success are running the same basic setup: a bank sinker or breakaway weight rig to get the bait down fast, a whole squid or squid-and-strip combo, glow beads or a small light stick up the leader to draw fish up out of the dark, and patience once you're at depth. This isn't a jig-and-hope game. It's drop, wait, watch the rod tip, and be ready when it finally loads up. Boats that treated it as a full-day commitment rather than a quick drop on the way to somewhere else are the ones with fish to show for it.

Looking at the next few days, the moon's easing off its new-phase pull, which should settle the tidal energy some and, if the pattern holds the way these things usually do, keep the swordfish stacked rather than scattering them. That's the case for staying with it if you've got the fuel and the weather window — a stable setup right now is worth more than chasing a new one. The bigger risk is a breakdown in that water structure that's been holding the fish; if the bite goes quiet at Oceanographer, the smart move is checking in with the fleet before burning fuel guessing at Hydrographer or Veatch blind. Best case, this swordfish window holds through the week and maybe extends toward Atlantis, shortening the run for boats out of the western Rhode Island ports. Worst case, it tapers the way these bites sometimes do once the moon settles, and the fleet has to go looking again. Either way, if you've only got one weather window this month for a long run, this is the one to spend it on — the swordfish story has been the real one out here, and it hasn't shown signs of quitting yet.
